newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: China warns Philippines over flag on shoal.
newsitem.headline: China warns Philippines over flag on shoal.

text.p: China said on Tuesday the raising of a Philippine flag on a disputed rock in the South China Sea was "a serious violation" of sovereignty and warned that a repeat would strain relations.
Chinese embassy spokesman Hao Yinbiao said in a statement the Scarborough Shoal belonged to China and the international community had never before challenged China's claim.

"It belongs to China's Zhongsha Islands (Macclesfield Bank) and is not at all a disputed island," Hao said. "Actions of the Philippine side have constituted a serious violation of China's territorial sovereignty.
"We hope that the Philippine side will refrain from any move to complicate the situation so as to maintain the overall Sino-Philippine friendly relations, which find roots in historical traditions."
Beijing protested to Manila last week after local fishermen raised the Philippine flag and removed Chinese markers on Scarborough Shoal on April 30 to assert Philippine sovereignty.

The Philippines also sent naval ships to the area to "unjustifiably disrupt joint international amateur radio exploration activities on the island organised by a non-governmental organisation of China", Hao said.
The shoal lies west of Zambales province just north of Manila and is not part of the Spratly Islands, a cluster of potentially oil-rich isles and reefs that Beijing says entirely belongs to China.
The Spratlys are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
Hao said China had been trying to enhance bilateral relations and "sincerely hopes that the Philippine government could...properly handle the existing issues between the two countries".

Last month the Philippines protested to China against the sending of what Manila said were armed Chinese naval ships near two islands in the Spratlys claimed by Manila. Beijing said the ships were on a research mission and withdrew them after a week.
Philippine navy chief Eduardo Santos denied Manila press reports that the navy planned to set up bases on areas claimed by Manila in the Spratlys to prevent future Chinese intrusions.
He said if ever facilities were built on the islands, they would be to "enhance the habitability" of Filipino troops assigned there.
Such facilities could also be used to convert "said islands into tourist spots or for other scientific, ecological and economic purposes", Santos said in a statement.
